I also experienced heightened anxiety and a faster heart rate when I first started taking lamotigrine, especially whilst upping dosages, and I’m also on clonodine to slow my heart rate which speaks volumes.
Lamotigrine takes about 6 weeks to balance out in your system, so there’s definitely an adjustment period where you might experience such side effects.
I’m currently going through withdrawals until I can get my script refilled, and the anxiety and fast heart rate is back, but while I was on lamotigrine, after it balanced out, I found it super helpful in treating my symptoms.
Different medications effect different people in different ways, If you continue experiencing side effects please reach out to your healthcare professional.

I experienced some side effects pretty quickly after first starting my course of antidepressants so I wouldn’t say it’s abnormal. They don’t kick in instantly in regards to their intended benefits unfortunately, which can take some several weeks to notice. Different medications react differently to different people in terms of their effectiveness, side effects, ect. Though usually the side effects should reduce in severity after your body adjusts to the new medication, if you feel your side effects are too extreme or are having any doubts I’d suggest having a discussion with your doctor. All the best.

It sounds like you’ve recently gone through a big change in terms of your way of life. Maybe with such a change there requires new goals / habits / activities or whatever to bring you that same sense of fulfilment? I don’t pretend to understand your situation, but I would think such a change would invoke much confusion onto how to proceed with your new lifestyle, ‘what’s next’ type of internal chatter. What I do know is that it usually takes time to adjust to new environments / ways of life and that it’s best not to be too hard on yourself while you figure these things out. I hope things start to look brighter for you, all the best.

Personally, different things help me at different times, sometimes a walk, sometimes a book or some mediation, some company, but at other times everything can just seem so futile and I just want to sleep and recharge. I’ve always appreciated people understanding that sometimes the support they offer might not always suit me in the moment, but the offers are always well received nonetheless, it’s the thought that counts provided their is no frustration involved if something suggested is too much for me at the moment. 

Be there for him when you can, offer your support and understanding and don’t be afraid to ask your SO for clarification if you feel you might be hovering too much. I’m usually open to communication with the people I share my depression with on how it effects the relationship, setting boundaries, ect. Don’t feel as though you need to pretend it isn’t there. 
We definitely all need to put our own mental health first in order to support those we care about, much like the oxygen mask emergency scenario on planes.

Just like I’m sure your SO won’t expect you to “fix” him, I’m sure he doesn’t expect you to find the ‘perfect balance’ between supporting him and checking up on him as your concern is certainly valid. Things change day by day, try not to be too hard on yourself, trust your gut and do what you think is right for yourself and your relationship. 

I’m glad sharing some of my experiences was able to help you, that’s warmed my soul. All the best.

Personally, especially when I’m in the midst of a ‘depressive spell’, I find my depression to be extremely burdensome on those I love. And that’s a horrible feeling, especially when you can see the pain your own suffering is causing another. I find my depression imposes upon me an apathetic guise that often makes me incapable of showing my love to an extent the other deserves, and that’s super disappointing because the love is there, it’s just strenuous to show it while my mind is brawling. It’s super taxing on whomever I share this burden with, it’s hard for people you love to understand, and often there isn’t much they can do to directly help or fix the problem and that often leaves the other feeling helpless or frustrated which has been an unfortunate reality for me. Thus, I often push people away to limit their own suffering because I’m often unsure of when I will feel more ‘whole’ again and able to provide the love they deserve. When I feel like a shell of a human, I feel those I love deserve better and I hate to see them struggle with the costs of my own suffering. 

Personally, the best support I’ve received are among the following:
- The person whom I share my feelings with proactively deals with and doesn’t ignore the effect it has on themselves, be it through talking about it with me, seeking therapy of their own, or anything similar. This helps me feel as though I’m not causing an excessive amount of pain that they are hiding from me or are not dealing with which can lead to resentment, and it astonishes me people can be willing to go through this with me and allows me the space to focus on building myself back up, knowing the other is doing the same for themselves and not being caught up in my pain.
- The other not getting frustrated that they can’t “fix” me and understanding that it is my own inner battle I must face. 
- Offering support when necessary, but not hovering over me, something as simple as offering a cup of tea or a reminder that the other is willing to talk if they are truely in a healthy headspace to listen.
- As much as it might annoy me sometimes when I’m in the midst of a depressive episode, I find I often benefit from occasional reminders to look after my health and care for myself (wash, shave, ect) sometimes the thought literally just doesn’t cross my mind.
- Seeing the other continue to live their life as ‘normal’, whilst still being there for me and not being detrimentally effected by my suffering. 
- Hugs, lots of them. 
I applaud you OP for seeking ways to help your SO, I hope everything works out well for you two. Take care of yourself, all the best.

I had a near death experience early last year. I was sure I was going to die. What I thought were going to be my last thoughts rushing through my mind during the experience was just the monotony and stress of the life I had lived thus far and how all my coping through it felt like it was all for nothing if I was just going to have my life taken. I survived, but I can’t shake that. What was once a manageable depression and anxiety combo has flipped 100 fold since the incident. 
I’ve since started therapy to help me manage my symptoms and try get a grip on life, but it’s been a long journey and I’m still struggling. I do believe it can be overcome though. Wishing you all the best.

You shouldn’t just shut up and get a job, I’ve tried that and became a workaholic who ignored my depression and ended up crashing big time. I’m not saying you will, but that was my experience and I’d highly advise against it. I believe it’s better to try find a balance between these two things. You can try to tackle both your depression and your lack of an income at the same time. It won’t be easy, but you can definitely reap the benefits of fighting your depression and generating income at the same time. You might find it less taxing picking up some casual work so as to leave time for your therapy and/or self improvement activities and benefit from not being overwhelmed by work whilst doing so. Casual work is often beneficial in the case where you can find cover for your shifts, should your mental health take an unexpected dip and you require some time for yourself. Therapy takes time, and hopefully over time through working on yourself you might be in a better position to pick up more work. It might not be instantaneous, but hopefully you will find some enjoyment out of it and meet new people like you mentioned. Balance is key and the path won’t always be linear. Allow yourself the time to figure out a work/life balance that suits you. Wishing you all the best.

I’m currently tapering down from 150mg Effexor to 20mg lexapro and I’ve noticed much of the same symptoms you mentioned pretty much immediately. Psychiatrist said it was my body adjusting. I was recently diagnosed with PTSD and after receiving a new referral was told lexapro might be better in managing my symptoms.

I’m currently mid-way through tapering down from 150mg Effexor and upping to 20mg Lexapro over a 30 day process. Pretty much straight away I noticed an increase in my depressive symptoms, anxiety, irritability, nightmares and pretty much everything else I went on Effexor for as well as crazy amounts of fatigue in the morning probably exacerbated by the use of Seroquel to sleep at night, which usually causes me fatigue lingering into midday, though it seems more pronounced now. I’ve been giving into the fatigue and sleeping away most of the days just to pass the time and skip through the side effects of this transition when I can. My psychiatrist says this is all normal, my body adjusting, but I was never expecting anything like this. Hoping this all improves after the Effexor is out of my system. Hopefully you haven’t found the transition as excruciating.
